clue.text: Shocked by not making a profit from writing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: so stunned you cannot speak

definitions.text: not making a profit from writing
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: losing money on what you write

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the phrase: 'at a loss' is trading unprofitably, and 'for words' is what an author sells.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone too stunned to speak is idiomatically lost for anything to say, which is what being shocked does.

clue.text: Badly upsetting fool, he makes a mistake

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the words that follow are put into a mangled order

parts.note: all fifteen letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A clumsy man offends an idiot and so commits a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'Badly' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: An accidental spoken error, saying the wrong word without meaning to, is one particular kind of mistake.

clue.text: Worker gets up to tricks in gym

parts.note: a hand is a manual labourer, as in farmhand
rises to your feet

explanation.surface: An employee gets up to mischief in the gymnasium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets up to tricks' reads as misbehaving; the split comes after 'gets up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Balancing upside down on your palms is a standard gymnastic exercise, one of the stunts performed in a gym.

clue.text: After this point, learnt about being constant

indicators.note: to bring something about is to turn it around, so the letters of the next word get moved

parts.note: east, one of the compass points
the letters of this word, rearranged

explanation.surface: From now on, the lesson someone has absorbed stays with them for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the rearranged letters after the compass point; 'this point' reads like a moment in time but is a direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting never changes or ends, so it is unfailingly constant.

clue.text: Love to write when free

parts.note: a score of zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
to pen a letter is to write it

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys writing whenever they have spare time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unrestricted or available to all, like an open meeting, is free in that sense.

clue.text: Praises variety of organic nuts a lot

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the following letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Someone raves about a range of organic nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Praises' looks like a verb but is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Expressions of approval and good wishes for an achievement are compliments, the plural noun sense of praises.

clue.text: Flying companions?

parts.note: surface reading: fellow travellers on an aeroplane
setter's reading: flocking creatures of one kind, the idiom for people of similar character who stick together

explanation.walkthrough: The saying is that like-minded people flock together, so the companions are literal fliers.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people of the same sort who keep company, pictured as winged creatures in one flock.

clue.text: Supporter beginning to accept law reform

indicators.note: to reform is to form again in a new shape, so the word before it is rearranged
to accept something is to take it in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: the start is the beginning
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: A backer is starting to come round to changing the legislation.
explanation.definitionFit: A loyal, dependable backer of a team or party is called a stalwart, the noun sense of a firm supporter.

clue.text: Reward academic with it

parts.note: short for professor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Give a scholar something in return, along with this.
explanation.definitionFit: A gain or benefit received from something is its reward, as in profiting from experience.

clue.text: Inclined to associate sentimental nonsense with man

parts.note: slop is gushing, mawkish writing or talk
a man's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: Someone tends to link mushy rubbish with men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclined to' reads as 'tending to', but 'Inclined' alone is the definition, meaning tilted.
explanation.definitionFit: A surface set at an angle rather than level is tilted, the physical sense of inclined.

clue.text: Grenade explodes beside eastern dissident

indicators.note: an explosion blows a thing apart, so the word before it lands in a scattered order

parts.note: the letters of this word rearranged
standard abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: A bomb goes off next to a rebel from the east.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade deserts or rebels against their own side, so is a dissident from its accepted line.

clue.text: When one loudly makes a disbelieving remark?

parts.note: as in 'as I left', meaning when
the Roman numeral for one
f stands for forte, loud, in music

explanation.surface: Asks when a person speaking at high volume voices scepticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loudly' hints at speech, but it is the musical mark for loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as a scornful retort, the phrase means 'that will never happen', an exclamation of disbelief.

clue.text: Linguist practices without one subsequently, I hear

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken out of the word before it

parts.note: to practise is to train
the Roman numeral for one, the letter taken out

indicators.note: what someone hears is a sound, so the result is matched by how it is said, not spelt

parts.note: later means afterwards; spoken, it matches the end of the answer

explanation.surface: A language expert says they will rehearse alone afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, 'trans later' sounds like the answer. 'Practices' is the American spelling of the verb practise.
explanation.definitionFit: A translator renders text from one language into another, so is a linguist by profession.

clue.text: Head girl brought in to act as guide at venue

indicators.note: something brought in is placed inside, so it goes within the phrase that follows

parts.note: to show someone round is to guide them

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the next word counts

parts.note: the first letter of girl

explanation.surface: A head girl is brought along to lead visitors around a site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head girl' looks like a school role; it is the first letter of 'girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: A showground is an open site where fairs and agricultural shows are held, a kind of venue.

clue.text: Not on the cards to be rude

parts.note: off is the opposite of on
the cards a player holds form a hand

explanation.surface: Being impolite is not something likely to happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on the cards' is an idiom for unlikely, but it splits into two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An offhand manner is curt and casually dismissive, which is impolite.

clue.text: Liked turning up when cold outside

indicators.note: something on the outside wraps around, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: polar regions are freezing

indicators.note: turning round makes a word face the other way, so its letters are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed showing up whenever the weather was chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or thing widely liked and admired by many people is popular.

clue.text: End programme after advertiser cancelled

parts.note: a sign advertises a shop or business
an event that is off has been cancelled

explanation.surface: A broadcast finishes once its sponsor has been dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasters sign off when they close a show or end transmission, so it means to finish a programme.

clue.text: Taking issue with professional examination

parts.note: short for professional
testing is examining

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a professional exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking issue with' looks like one phrase; the split falls before 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: To protest is to object, the same as disputing or arguing against something.

clue.text: Tip unknown to take off first

indicators.note: first tells the solver which part comes in front when the two parts are joined

parts.note: to ape someone is to mimic them, to take them off
x is an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: An anonymous hint about removing something before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests removal; here it means imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: The apex is the very top or pointed end of something, its tip.

clue.text: Styled hair when exhausted?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: hair worn loose, not put up
second meaning: tired out by constant pressure

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the first meaning is a playful literal reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ground down by strain leaves a person weary, which is the idiomatic sense of exhausted.

clue.text: Goatherd keeps promise

indicators.note: something that keeps another holds it inside, so the answer sits within the word before

parts.note: letters two to five of this word

explanation.surface: A shepherd of goats stays true to their word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps promise' reads as honouring a pledge, but 'keeps' is the holding signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A solemn vow, often sworn, is a formal promise.

clue.text: Substance of work consumed one beforehand

indicators.note: beforehand says the numeral is placed in front of the word for eaten when the parts are joined

parts.note: short for opus, a work
the Roman numeral for one
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: The core of the job ate one up earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beforehand' says the one comes before 'consumed' in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a drug derived from opium, a narcotic substance.

clue.text: Adapt to modern times perfectly

parts.note: AD, anno domini, marks the current era
as in 'just right', exactly

explanation.surface: Fit in with the present day flawlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adapt to' looks like one phrase, but 'to' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To adjust is to modify or alter to suit new conditions, the same as adapting.

clue.text: Funds can transfer without penalties

indicators.note: to transfer is to move things over, so the letters of the word before are shifted around
without here means outside, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: fines are monetary penalties
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: Money can be moved without incurring charges.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's or body's finances are its money resources, the funds it has available.
